PRESENTATION OF OIL PAINTING DEPICTING FATHERS OF CONFEDERATION
speechtext:
Order. On the eve of the 98th anniversary of Canada's Confederation I ask leave to make an announcement of interest and importance to all hon. Members, which should be of significance to all Canadians.
In the tragic fire of 1916 that destroyed the old Centre Block we lost one of the finest historical treasures, the monumental oil painting by Robert Harris of the Fathers of Confederation. That famous painting, which only exists now in copy, depicts the Quebec Conference of 1864. I know all hon. Members will be delighted to learn that an exact restoration of the Robert Harris painting is to be presented to the nation by Confederation Life Association. It will be hung in the Parliament Buildings, hopefully well before July 1, 1967. The artist commissioned for this challenging task is Mr. Rex Woods, of Toronto, who is noted for his portrayal of persons and events from Canada's past.
The success of our forthcoming centennial hinges on the imagination and leadership of government at all levels, voluntary and other organizations, business and individuals. I am sure this gift to the nation from Confederation Life will help to make Canadian history come alive, both for our own people and for those of other lands.

FEDERAL IMPLEMENTATION OF PROVINCIAL AGREEMENTS WITH FOREIGN COUNTRIES
speechtext:
1.	On what occasions since July 1, 1867 has the Government of Canada been requested by any of the provincial governments for an intergovernmental exchange to implement an entente, or an accord or an agreement entered into by a province and a foreign power respecting matters within provincial jurisdiction?
2.	Briefly, what was the subject-matter in each case?

speakeroldname: Mr. Stanley Haidasz (Parliamentary Secretary to Secretary of State for External Affairs):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: FEDERAL IMPLEMENTATION OF PROVINCIAL AGREEMENTS WITH FOREIGN COUNTRIES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the answer to the first part is as follows: Until approximately 40 years ago the occasion for a request of the nature specified in the question would not have arisen under the Canadian constitution. Any interest which a province might have had in participating in arrangements with other governmental entities was a matter falling within the sphere of responsibility of Her Majesty's Government in the United Kingdom. All arrangements concerning matters falling within provincial legislative jurisdiction and purporting to have effect beyond the boundaries of the province were either embodied in Empire treaties or were in the nature of internal arrangements between the various parts of the Empire. The constitutional position prevailing until then, coupled with the fact that in the meantime the provinces have only infrequently seen the need in practice for formal arrangements to be entered into with foreign countries on matters within their legislative jurisdiction, has meant that there have been few occasions in practice when the provinces have found it necessary to seek the assistance of the federal Government in this respect.
The answer to the second part is as follows. In 1958 the federal Government was asked by the Government of New Brunswick to facilitate the conclusion of an agreement by that province and the state of Maine for the construction of the Campobello-Lubec bridge. A similar request was received from the province of Ontario in 1959 in connection with an agreement to be entered into between that province and the state of Minnesota for the construction of a bridge over the Pigeon River. Details of the two occasions since
June 30, 1965

April 1963 on which the Government of Canada facilitated the arrangements between the province of Quebec and France have already been given to the House in answer to question No. 2,768 asked by the hon. Member for Edmonton West on February 23, 1965. The text of this answer can be found on page 11818 of Hansard for March 1, 1965. Since then the federal Government has been requested by the province of New Brunswick to facilitate the conclusion of an agreement between that province and the state of Maine for the construction of a bridge across the St. Croix River at Milltown.

subtopic: 'LEGALIZATION OF LOTTERIES
speechtext:
The most
recent expression of Government inten-

tion on this subject was contained in the press release following the federal-provincial conference held in November, 1963, as follows:
"Some provincial governments explained the difficulties they have in enforcing the provisions of the Criminal Code in respect of lotteries and gambling. speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish to address a question to the Minister

June 30, 1965
Inquiries of the Ministry of Labour. In view of the strong protest launched by the U.A.W. against the newly announced TAB plan, and the recent strong protest from the Ford Motor Company, both of whom are directly affected, can the Minister of Labour say whether he is prepared to withdraw this plan and put forward a better plan which would be acceptable to both parties concerned?

speakeroldname: Hon. A. J. MacEachen (Minister of Labour):
subtopic: ASSISTANCE TO WORKERS AND INDUSTRIES
subsubtopic: AFFECTED BY AUTOMOBILE AGREEMENT
speechtext: No, Mr. Speaker, it is not intended to withdraw the plan. The plan is a good plan. It provides a very high level of benefits. It compares very favourably with the plan proposed in the United States, and in the circumstances I think it is quite proper to expect the Ford Motor Company to contribute to a fund to assist in the adjustment problems of these workers. Because of the care that has been taken in developing this plan; because it provides a high level of benefits for the workers; because it holds intact their SUB funds and benefits for the future, and because it places an obligation on the companies to contribute, I think it ought to be acceptable generally after this is fully understood.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
subtopic: ASSISTANCE TO WORKERS AND INDUSTRIES
subsubtopic: AFFECTED BY AUTOMOBILE AGREEMENT
speechtext: A supplementary question, Mr. Speaker. How does the Minister justify his statement that this is a good plan when both parties who are subject to the plan are protesting against it?

subtopic: ASSISTANCE TO WORKERS AND INDUSTRIES
subsubtopic: AFFECTED BY AUTOMOBILE AGREEMENT
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I understand the attitude of the Ford Motor Company. It is an attitude that would be fully understood, but from the point of view of the public it is important in our view that the companies be given an opportunity to bear a part of this financial burden.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
subtopic: ASSISTANCE TO WORKERS AND INDUSTRIES
subsubtopic: AFFECTED BY AUTOMOBILE AGREEMENT

subsubtopic: AFFECTED BY AUTOMOBILE AGREEMENT
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, it would be unusual for the leadership of a trade union to accept fully any plan without suggesting that the benefits be higher and the reaction in this instance is fully understood and expected.

speechtext: On the orders of the day:

subtopic: VANCOUVER ISLAND-COMPENSATION FOR LOSS OF NURSERY STOCK THROUGH INFESTATION
speechtext: wish to address a question to the Minister of Agriculture which is of concern to some agricultural producers in British Columbia. Can the Minister inform the House what his Department has done to meet the problem of the golden nematode, which has been bothering some farmers in British Columbia?

speakeroldname: Hon. Harry W. Hays (Minister of Agriculture):
subtopic: VANCOUVER ISLAND-COMPENSATION FOR LOSS OF NURSERY STOCK THROUGH INFESTATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as hon. Members are aware, the department announced on June 22 that the golden nematode, a serious pest of potato and tomato crops, had been found in a commercial field of potatoes in the Saanich peninsula of Vancouver Island.
This is a serious pest, not only because of its effect on potato crops but because if it became widespread it could result in restrictions on exports of plants with soil and seed potatoes, particularly to the United States.
The nematode was identified on the Vancouver Island farm on June 17. The farm has been placed under quarantine, and the export out of Canada of plants or crops with soil from Vancouver Island has been prohibited. Departmental officials have conducted an intensive survey of crops on the peninsula and to date have found no further indications of infestation except on this one farm. Investigations, however, are being continued to ensure that the infestation is confined to this one farm.
With regard to the question raised by the hon. Member for Esquimalt-Saanich, I may say that in cases where it is warranted appropriate compensation is provided for under the Destructive Insect and Pest Act.

subtopic: VANCOUVER ISLAND-COMPENSATION FOR LOSS OF NURSERY STOCK THROUGH INFESTATION

The other thing I want to ask the Minister about is apropos his statement yesterday

that the interest was not a serious factor, but that the real problem involved is getting capital. It seems to me that 6 per cent is a fairly high rate of interest. If the Minister is really interested in helping the small auto parts manufacturers in this process of economic dislocation, the Government can certainly borrow money for less than that, and I wonder why the Minister does not consider 5 per cent as an appropriate rate. I think the only advantage that can be gained under the present terms is the one mentioned by the Minister yesterday, that they can borrow from this fund, assuming it is not all used up in the first six months, whereas they might have greater difficulty borrowing from financial institutions. I would think that most of the companies, with the security they have, would not have much difficulty in borrowing money at 6 per cent. The way the Minister could really help them would be by making this money available at a lower interest rate.
I have asked the Minister two questions; one, what is the estimate based on and, second, will he consider making this money available to these small parts manufacturers at a lower rate of interest?

speakerposition: Minister of Industry; Minister of Defence Production
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, dealing with the questions asked, first as to the interest rate, let me say that the object of this legislation is not to put the Government into competition with normal commercial credit granting facilities, but merely to provide those motorcar parts manufacturers, who find that they are for one reason or another not satisfactory commercial risks, with an alternative source of capital for financing their changes and expansions. It is not intended that this legislation should be a special form of subsidy to parts manufacturers in the sense of giving them-those who avail themselves of these loans-a lower rate of interest, or cheaper money than their competitors can get elsewhere. This legislation is not intended to put the Government into competition with normal commercial credit facilities.

May I ask the Minister a question on that point. Have the Minister's investigations shown that 6 per cent is about the average interest rate which manufacturers of this type would pay if they borrowed money on the commercial market? I thought they could borrow money at 5J or 54 per cent.

speakerposition: Minister of Industry; Minister of Defence Production
speechtext:
I am not in the borrowing business myself, Mr. Chairman, but I only wish that motorcar manufacturers in Canada could
June 30. 1965

borrow money at 5J per cent on short term. Unfortunately that is not the case. The 6 per cent interest on relatively short-term borrowings is an attractive rate of interest.
You refer to short-term borrowing. What term has the Minister in mind?

speakerposition: Minister of Industry; Minister of Defence Production
speechtext:
I have in mind relatively short or medium-term borrowing. Obviously longterm money tends to be cheaper than medium or short-term money.
In so far as the estimate is concerned, it is quite frankly just that, an estimate obtained after canvassing, to the extent possible, the not fully formulated plans of the motorcar parts manufacturers. It is hoped that this will be more than enough. As the hon. Member for Burnaby-Coquitlam suggests, the attractiveness of the expansion plans of most of the parts manufacturers-and it is apparent to the bankers and other money lenders in this country that they are in a substantially expanding market-is such that they are good risks, and it is expected there will be relatively little recourse to this fund.
The hon. Member for Wellington South asked what representations have been made by the parts manufacturing industry involved in the announcement of two days ago. In reply to that question, let me say that the first reaction is highly satisfactory. The Parts Manufacturers Association has indicated that this will meet their immediate needs and, of course, they are happy about it.

Mr. Chairman, I wonder whether I may be allowed to ask a couple of questions I forgot to ask earlier. Why did the Minister set this up as a separate organization, and why is this not being handled through the Industrial Development Bank? speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, as was pointed out in the announcement, the determiners who will say who shall get a loan, and who shall not get a loan, will be the members of the board set up for this purpose. Mr. Chairman, may I ask two

speechtext:

speechtext: This was pointed out in the announcement I made. In respect of loans secured by moveables, to use Quebec terminology, the maximum period will be of the order of 10 years and in respect of loans secured by immoveable, 20 years.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
Order, please. May I suggest that we allow the hon. Member for Villeneuve to make a contribution to the debate.

Mr. Chairman, I just wish to ask the Minister of Industry a few questions.
It seems to me that there is a duplication in administration by this new estimate and the way the minister is explaining to Parliament the application of this act dealing with loans, investments and advances to the automobile parts manufacturers. Will people who need such funds be able to borrow from the Industrial Development Bank which exists already? Will they be able also to borrow from another credit or banking institution with the government underwriting those loans?
It is important to know how the department intends to go about administering those loans granted to industrialists and new industries.
The creation of a special commission has been announced to deal with that matter. Special commissions are already operating within the Industrial Development Bank. I believe that some people there are already used to dealing with the industrial and economic development of Canada. We just have to give them more leeway and increase their present responsibilities. Then, there will not be any administrative duplication and the Industrial Development Bank could very well loan funds on a standard basis provided they get the authorization from the department.
I should like to know exactly how the people in need of that money will proceed: will they go to the Industrial Development Bank or to other banking institutions? How will the funds then be provided by the government? Will it not give a guarantee to a banking institution or to the Industrial Development Bank, or will the funds granted by the government be loaned to those new industries which we shall help keep in operation?

speakerposition: Minister of Industry; Minister of Defence Production
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, the choice will lie in the first instance with the borrower. For reasons of his own he may prefer to use his customary means of securing additional capital, and there are a variety of choices open to him. If he is already a client of the Industrial Development Bank he may wish to avail himself of the facilities of that institution. There is of course a somewhat higher rate of interest payable and a somewhat shorter term normally required by the Industrial Development Bank than the rate of interest prescribed and the length of the term
[The Chairman.]
of the loan provided for in this particular arrangement.
When consideration was given to the establishment of a separate loan fund and a separate board as an alternative to employing entirely the facilities of the Industrial Development Bank it was felt that for a short term operation, as was made clear in the announcement that this form of assistance both on the side of industrial capital and on the side of labour would extend only to 1968, it would be preferable to set up a separate authorizing body to take care of the short term arrangement rather than endeavouring to change the practices and policies of the Industrial Development Bank.
Mr. Chairman, how many members-

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order, please, The hon. Member for Villeneuve.

Mr. Speaker, does the minister not admit, then, that there is duplication in the administration? Would it not have been simpler to authorize the Industrial Development Bank to deal with such cases, thus materially reducing the total cash expense or operating costs which this new administration will cost the Canadian people? Why not, instead, amend the act that now governs the Industrial Development Bank to allow it to make such transactions?

speakerposition: Minister of Industry; Minister of Defence Production
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, there will be no duplication of administration. As I pointed out, the administration and servicing of the loans will be carried out by the staff of the Industrial Development Bank and the only additional body that will be created will be this particular board consisting of a chairman and a number of senior civil servants who will be taking on this task in addition to their present functions. The reason for doing it this way rather than changing the statute of the Industrial Development Bank for a short period was that it was felt we should not disorganize for a short-term project the practices of the Industrial Development Bank which have been evolved over a long period.

Mr. Chairman, I have only a few comments to make. I must say I take some exception to the method by which this matter is brought before the House. It may be that time is of the essence and that the exigencies of the situation are such that
June 30, 1965

this action is required. If that is the case, then this action is to some extent understandable. I took exception to the way in which the original measure was introduced by Order in Council; I take exception to the way moneys are made available for the purpose of assisting those who will be displaced in connection with the labour situation, and I take the same stand with regard to the way in which these loans are going to be made.
My view is that matters of this kind where we are breaking new ground should all have been brought forward in legislative form. With regard to the organizations which have been mentioned, the Industrial Development Bank, the Farm Credit Corporation, the Export Credits Insurance Corporation, and so on, legislation was brought before the House and conditions were laid down categorically. The House had ample opportunity to discuss those measures and to make such changes and recommend such alterations as they saw fit.
This particular vote is in the most general terms. The vote as such is a resolution of the House and when incorporated in an appropriation bill it becomes a statute. It seems to me that matters of this kind should be embodied in a vehicle dealing with the issues, particularly where there is a radical departure from the practice of the past.
I notice it is suggested that despite the Financial Administration Act there may be total commitments of $20 million, but my experience is that once such votes creep into the estimates they are continued year in and year out. We may be establishing a precedent here which will make it difficult in the future for us to take objection with regard to issues of this kind. I am not going to argue about the desirability of or necessity for this action, but the method used in this instance and in connection with the vote of $5 million for the original program is one in respect of which I must register my strong protest.

I just wanted to say a word in support of the position taken by the hon. Member for Peace River and to register our objection as well to the manner in which this particular type of legislation has been brought before the House. After all, $20 million is a great deal of money, yet we are handed an executive decision by way of an announcement on orders of the day. It seems to us no adequate way is provided for dealing with the matter in this particular fashion. I should like to endorse his views and place this party on record in this matter.
We know the Minister of Industry is very able and knows everything about matters of this kind. Perhaps we should not be questioning his judgment. At the same time, however, we have a good example in the bills which we were discussing on orders of the day again, and about which it seems the views of the Opposition are not really very important and are not going to be given very much consideration. 5c. To extend the purposes of Labour Vote 5, Main Estimates, 1965-66 to include authority for payments

June 30, 1965
Supply-Labour
of transitional assistance, in accordance with regulations approved by the Governor in Council, to workers in automotive manufacturing and parts industries who become unemployed as a result of the operation of the Canada-United States Agreement on Automotive Products, $5,000,000.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: We were holding this item until the Minister of Labour arrived, in case he wanted to make a statement further to the announcement he made earlier.

Mr. Chairman, I do not intend to take much of the time of the committee in introducing this item. I will be prepared to answer any questions that may arise in connection with the item that is being put forward to provide transitional assistance for auto workers. We believe that the automotive agreement will increase production and employment in the automotive industry. The automotive agreement involves considerable reorganization of production, and for that reason there will be temporary unemployment and displacement of workers in the automobile manufacturing industry and in the parts industry. We do not believe that the workers should bear the full burden, the full financial burden, of their unemployment. The economy as a whole will benefit, the country as a whole will benefit, the automobile companies will benefit, and for that reason we believe it is reasonable that the taxpayers and the companies jointly should assist the workers over this temporary period of unemployment.
We are providing a level of benefits for eligible workers ranging from 62 per cent to 75 per cent of the workers' weekly pay, depending upon the number of their dependants and provided these benefits do not exceed 65 per cent of the average weekly wages and salaries in the motor vehicle and motor vehicle parts industries. The present average is just about $75 per week. The maximum benefit available under this proposed plan is $75 per week. I think the generosity, which is the wrong word in the circumstances, in increasing the level of benefit provided under this plan can be more readily appreciated if it is compared with the maximum level of benefit available to unemployed workers under unemployment insurance, which is $36 per week. The maximum under this plan is $75 per week. The maximum hitherto accepted in this country, accepted by Parliament under a bill introduced by my predecessor is $36 per week. We have made, therefore, very successful strides in increasing the level of benefits which will be not only of importance in this case but which will be a point of

comparison for any future changes in unemployment insurance, and any further extension of this principle to other cases.

May I ask the Minister a
question while he is on that point? How would this maximum of $75 compare with the maximum which would be available to unemployed auto workers who have SUB, because that is the only fair comparison-not with the general unemployment insurance figure?

This plan will provide a level of benefit slightly higher than SUB-$2 or $3 higher. Now, bear in mind that this plan will apply to all auto workers, many of whom presently are not covered by SUB plans. The taxpayer will have to bear the additional burden of this transitional payment because many are not eligible for SUB plans.

In the event you are making payments to workers who are not eligible for SUB benefit, is it not a fact that they will not be eligible for TAB unless the employer agrees to pay into the fund what he would have paid if they had been eligible for SUB payments?

No, Mr. Chairman; we are not in this plan worsening or bettering the position of any company. We asked companies with SUB plans that an amount equivalent will be put into the treasury or into the TAB fund equivalent to what the company would have paid to it if the SUB plan had been used. In plants where no SUB plan exists-the smaller parts companies, in many cases-there will be no contribution forthcoming from companies. Contributions will come only from companies with SUB plans. [DOT] (4:00 p.m.)

Take for example the case of the lay-offs in Windsor last week end. Some 500 workers were laid off by a company which has a SUB plan. Because these men had been employed for less than a year they were not eligible for SUB payments in any event. Are they eligible for TAB even though the employer does not contribute?

Yes, they will be eligible if they meet the requirements. No doubt we shall be discussing these later.
I think it is important to say a word about our attitude toward the SUB funds. Representations were made to the Government by the auto workers to the effect that these funds, which are built up by company contributions, had at a certain stage in the evolution of
June 30. 1965

collective bargaining been gained in lieu of wage increases. The argument was put forward: Why should these SUB funds be used during a lay-off induced by public action? We accepted that argument. The proposal of the United States was different. They intend to use the SUB funds. The reason we accepted the argument is simple. If the SUB funds were used to pay benefits during this lay-off the duration and level of benefits would be affected in subsequent lay-offs. In other words, less would be available for use by the workers in non-Government-induced lay-offs. We are therefore asking the companies which have SUB funds to pay into the TAB fund an amount equivalent to what they would have paid had the SUB fund been in operation. The credit of the workers will remain intact for the future, and for workers under any SUB plan the level of benefit will be the difference between what they would receive under unemployment insurance and the maximum of $75.
This is a very important feature of the proposal we are making. In the United States a determination of the benefits to the workers to be affected has not yet been made. A Congressional Committee has studied this question very carefully and a proposal is made in the Committee report indicating Congressional intent as to how public benefits ought to be related to the SUB plans. It may be that the level of benefits, immediately, may be higher than the maximum in Canada if Congressional intent is reflected in a decision of the arbitrator in the SUB plans. We limit our level of benefits to 65 per cent of the average weekly wages and salaries in the motor vehicle and motor vehicle parts industries. The limitation in the United States is, of course, the average of manufacture. The feature of this plan which is definitely superior is that the companies are being asked to pay up, to meet the cost of benefits during this transitional period and the workers will have the SUB plans intact, fully protected for subsequent lay-offs.
What if the companies do not pay up?

The hon. gentleman asks what would happen should the companies not participate. The Minister of Industry may have something to say about the company contributions, because discussions have taken place between his department and the Ford Motor Company. We fully expect that the motor companies will come forward and con-22620-197
Supply-Labour
tribute. And why not? They are receiving very handsome benefits from this plan.
I may say I am getting a lot of advice from hon. Members around me. This is a group speech.

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
There are a lot of
us here who are interested in Windsor.

The companies are receiving these benefits and we are not asking them to contribute more than they would be contributing had the SUB funds been in operation. The hon. Member for Burnaby-Coquit-lam says there is no compulsion. There is no compulsion legally, but surely there is a very strong social compulsion for the companies to come forward and contribute. I feel sure the companies will come forward.
What if they do not? What will happen to the workers in that case? Will TAB continue to pay the full amount?
I do not want to be flippant and say that this is a hypothetical question, but I do not expect to meet that situation at all. I am not thinking of the possibility of the companies not coming forward.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: On that very point, a few minutes ago the Minister of Labour said there were a great many people who were not covered under SUB. The reason they are not covered in most instances is the attitude taken by the companies that they were not prepared to enter into a collective agreement in this sphere. It was not for lack of bargaining by the U.A.W.A. designed to incorporate this into a collective agreement. If these companies were not prepared to enter into a collective agreement, how will the Minister persuade them to contribute a similar sum toward TAB? If they do refuse, where is the money coming from to pay those who may be affected?
Workers for companies under agreements not including SUB will be fully compensated out of the TAB fund.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: That is, by the Government.
They will be fully compensated out of the TAB fund provided by this estimate. Only companies with SUB funds will be asked to provide an equivalent amount.

Mr. Chairman, the minister has just told us in his own way the process that will be used with respect to adjustments

June 30, 1965
Supply-Labour
made for workers who will have to change jobs.
In the first place, who will decide the eligibility of workers? Will it be the National Employment Service or the Unemployment Insurance Commission? Which organization will decide the eligibility of a candidate or claimant who puts in an application to obtain such a sum of money?
The minister says that the management of automobile companies do not object to taking part in these payments. In this connection, I agree with him and even if some members have expressed their concern, we are not afraid of that. The companies will lose absolutely nothing, even if they contribute. Indeed, if the directors of a firm are contributing $100 for instance, do not suppose that this amount will be taken out of their profits. The price of the car will be increased not by $100, which was the amount provided, but by $100 plus the normal profit rate, namely 10, 12, 15 or 20 per cent, which means that the prices are going to be increased and that the Canadian taxpayer, the Canadian worker is again the one who will have to pay.
It could be the dealer.

Not even the dealer, Mr. Chairman. Those who are wondering whether the companies will share in this plan need not worry, for the directors of those companies agree right off with the minister or ministers concerned to contribute to those funds, since those contributions will be added to the cost price of the products they will be selling.
Consequently, I feel that the minister is perfectly right in saying that he is not worried, that he does not even think that those company officials could refuse to participate in his scheme. Anyone would contribute in the same way when it is profitable to him and does not cost a cent to the company.
Mr. Chairman, what will happen to the man, to the worker who will be displaced? Who will decide whether or not he is eligible to the benefits he is claiming because he is displaced or transferred from one plant to another?
[DOT] (4:10 p.m.)

Mr. Chairman, the hon. Member for Villeneuve asked how the eligibility of workers would be determined. An application for assistance could be submitted by a firm on behalf of its employees, by a group of workers, by their union or by an authorized representative, to the Adjustment

Assistance Board, and the Board would conduct an investigation and determine whether a significant number or proportion of workers of the firm or subdivision thereof have been or will be laid off for a period of at least 30 days, and whether the lay-off was caused by the termination of or significant decrease of production or activity arising from the operation of the Canada-United States automotive agreement. If the Board accepts the application it will then certify that this group of workers is eligible and the workers would then apply to the Department of Labour for the transitional assistance.
Is there any length of time involved?
The determination must be made within 30 days of receipt of the application by the Board.
Is there any length of service by the worker required in order for him to be eligible?

Yes, Mr. Chairman. The worker must first of all be eligible to receive unemployment insurance benefit. To be eligible a worker must have had at least 30 weeks of employment in the 52 weeks prior to the lay-off; the idea being that there must be some attachment to the industry on the part of a worker in order to receive benefit. This is well understood in unemployment insurance and other benefits, and 30 weeks is the period of employment that is required.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext:
With regard to the 30 days in which approval must be obtained from the Adjustment Assistance Board, is this period after the actual lay-off takes place?
Mr. MacEachen.' It is actually after the application has been received by the Board. Presumably an application could be made to the Board in anticipation of a lay-off, but more logically it would probably occur at the time of the lay-off. Then the application would be made, and the determination made within 30 days.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, the Minister of Labour has outlined to us in brief detail some of the aspects of this so-called new plan, the TAB plan. It is no different, in my opinion, from what has been negotiated with the employers by most of these people who will be affected. That is called the Supplementary Unemployment Benefits plan. The Minister said a moment ago that application must be made to the Adjustment Assistance
June 30, 1965

Board in respect of workers who have been laid off, and a decision must be made within 30 days. This is not good enough. This is not as good as the SUB plan, under which a person laid off can receive full benefit after the first seven days and does not have to wait. He can send his application directly to Ottawa in order to have it considered carefully, and does not have to wait 30 days without receiving any benefits whatever.
What does this new TAB plan really do? It gives each and every worker $2 or $3 a week more than he would receive under the SUB plan; but because of the limit of $75 a week many employees who have negotiated for a higher percentage under the SUB plan would receive less. Not only the automobile industry but subsidiary industries, parts manufacturers, operating under the SUB plan give anywhere up to 80 per cent or 85 per cent of the take-home pay of the worker. Consequently the worker is not going to receive as much under this plan as is the case under the regular SUB plan. No wonder the U.A.W, which negotiates most of these contracts, and all the automobile industry and its subsidiaries, are claiming that this plan is not the solution to their problem. It does not go far enough; in many cases it does not go as far as SUB.
What is the Government's contribution? It is $2 or $3 a week per worker. This is the entire contribution the Government is willing to make. You cannot count the unemployment insurance benefits because they are there now; the workers are entitled to them now, provided they have made sufficient contributions. What the Government is offering them is $2 or $3 a week more, in some instances, than they would get under the SUB. This measure, this supposedly great help to the laid-off workers, has been brought in as the direct result of an agreement this Government signed almost six months ago. Here is a Government which came into office on the basis of 60 days of decision. It has now become a Government of deadlines. I doubt very much whether even this token assistance would have been brought in if we were not approaching the end of the session and a recess for the summer months, if pressures had not built up to the extent that the Government was forced to do something about this very important matter.
The Ford Company of Canada points out the facts. I have not heard the Minister dispute these facts, which are contained in the Globe and Mail of today's date. In despair, 22620-1971
Supply-Labour
at the last minute and because of impending lay-offs in the Ford motorcar industry, the Minister of Labour rushes to Washington- and this is all he comes back with. I am sure he did not copy the American plan at all; he could have stayed at home and figured this out. All he had to do was to add $2 or $3 more to some of the existing SUB plans.
[DOT] (4:20 p.m.)
This is a last minute rush. We had the same situation with the Minister of Industry, who all of a sudden found out, after the Prime Minister had made an announcement on June 7, that he needed a bill to put into effect the principle enunciated by the Prime Minister. Here we are today faced with a problem which we have to unravel. This matter could have been decided two weeks ago. There has been negligence all down the line in the treasury benches on most of the matters affecting the country as a whole and its people.
George Burt of the United Automobile Workers, who is spokesman for the U.A.W.A. members, says that this step does not go far enough, and in view of this he is prepared to criticize the whole plan. I do not think that he would make a statement of that kind without some very serious consideration of the effects of the plan.
A few moments ago the hon. Member for Villeneuve asked who would be in charge of the fund and who would make the payments. I do not think that the Minister advised us as to the instrument he will use to make these payments, whether it would be the Unemployment Insurance Commission or some other agency. These are questions which the Minister of Labour should answer before we pass $5 million, which is a substitute for what should have been an effective plan for workers who are laid off as a direct result of this Government's agreement with the United States.
We should also consider the fact that because of the trade policies of the Government there may be lay-offs in other industries as a result. How does this affect other industries outside the automobile industry? What about lay-offs in the furniture industry, the aluminum industry or the textile industry? Is this plan going to be extended to these industries or is it exclusive to the automobile industry? I would ask the Minister of Labour to answer these questions also.

Mr. Chairman, I have a few general observations to make to the Minister,

June 30. 1965
Supply-Labour
and then perhaps we can get into the detailed questioning of the plan. First of all, it has been said before in this House that this party is in broad general agreement with the intent of this scheme. All parties in the House have been worried about the imbalance in the automotive industry between Canada and the United States, and the general intent of this legislation to try and correct this is a good one, one with which no one would take serious issue. But it seems to us that this agreement and the proposal of the Minister raises a far more serious question.
What we really have here is one of the first occasions where the actual trade policies of the Government have resulted or will result in fairly severe dislocation of the workers in the industries involved. These workers had nothing to do with the decisions which brought about their unemployment. The agreement was negotiated between the two Governments concerned and the employers. These workers had no influence or sway over our trade policies. As I said, I am not particularly quarrelling with them-
Neither did Parliament.

As my leader says, neither did Parliament-but be that as it may, the Government has initiated a very serious problem for the labour movement.
What we would suggest to the Minister is that we take this occasion to establish a new principle in our relations with the trade union movement, namely that where dislocation takes place in the labour force as a result of Government action the workers in the industries concerned should not be expected to bear any economic loss. It is not fair to equate the position with SUB benefits because, as the Minister knows, SUB benefits were never intended to meet this type of situation. Workers in the automotive industry know that there are likely to be lay-offs when they take jobs. This is a hazard of their occupation, and to protect them the union has built up these funds under the agreements. But there is no relationship at all between the principle of SUB plans and the principle as stated in this proposal.
Therefore, Mr. Chairman, we are suggesting it is important to establish this principle now because of its implications for the future, namely that economic dislocation caused by Government activity in the trade field should not result in any economic loss to workers engaged in particular industries. This is not a particularly new idea; there are other areas

where this principle has been accepted. But if the Government is not prepared seriously to consider this proposal I suggest there is a real danger that it will succeed in mobilizing the entire labour movement of Canada against any sort of long range and substantial trade policy dislocation.
Already Mr. Burt, the leader of the Auto Workers Union, has spoken out. The Minister said he was not surprised that the union did not feel the benefits were high enough, but because the benefits are so small they have now decided to go out and launch a national campaign to try and turn public opinion against this agreement. Why are they doing this? They are doing it because this Government will not accept the idea that if the community brings about dislocation for the general good then the community should pay the economic cost of such dislocation. We are asking these workers to pick up approximately 35 per cent of the TAB plan, because we have placed an upper limit of 65 per cent on their possible earnings. In effect, the Minister is saying to these workers that they must pay at least 35 per cent, or in other words take a 35 per cent slash in pay and, in addition, forfeit many of their fringe benefits if they are not compensated for them. So we think there is an extremely important principle involved at this time.
In other parts of the world this principle has been accepted. For example, in the European Coal and Steel Community there are provided tide-over allowances for workers, which run up to 100 per cent of their wages plus other forms of assistance, including supplementation or reduced wages. They may receive these benefits for up to two years. Because that guarantee has been given under the Treaty of Rome, the unions involved welcome any kind of automation dislocation or economic change that the Government may want to bring in. But unless you are prepared to accept this principle in Canada, every time the Government wants to bring about a major trade change it will have the labour movement involved mobilized against it, because of what I say is the very niggardly way the Government have adopted in dealing with the dislocation which will take place.
In the United States Secretary McNamara gave a flat undertaking, when the Government closed down 95 military bases, that the workers affected would receive their salaries, would be retrained if necessary, and
June 30, 1965

that the Government would pay the expenses of moving them, so that in effect they would suffer no economic dislocation at all. We would suggest to the Minister in all seriousness that if he is not prepared to accept this principle, then he is opening the door to a great deal of unrest between organized labour and the Government. I hope I am wrong in this contention, but the indications we have received from the trade union movement are that this will be the ultimate consequences of enacting this legislation unless some very substantial changes are made.
[DOT] (4:30 p.m.)
This was certainly borne out, Mr. Chairman, at the hearings in Washington when one of the senior officials of the U.A.W., Mr. Leonard Woodcock, Vice-President, testifying before the Committee said, as recorded at page 12 of his brief:
-it will be impossible to mobilize future labour movement support for trade liberalization unless and until it is demonstrated that meaningful assistance can and will be provided.
The United States Vice President of that union was laying down a warning to Government that unless almost complete protection is given, the labour force will rise up and resist the very changes and trade policies that many of us are convinced are going to be necessary if we are to adjust in the modern world.
We should look at the actual proposals themselves in order to back this up. As I have said, the first and most obvious one is the limitation. How do you justify telling a working man that because you are going to put him out of work, through no fault of his own, he is only going to get 65 per cent of his normal salary?
Seventy five per cent.

It could go as high as 75 per cent, provided that is not above the 65 per cent general average. However, even taking that figure, what is the working man going to do to get the balance? Why should he be required, because you have done something over which he has no control, to accept this slash in income? Most of these people, like all of us, have their incomes pretty well committed and cannot accept a 25 or 35 per cent slash in income.
The Minister was good enough to admit that even these benefits might appear generous over and above those paid under the Unemployment Insurance Fund, which have always been an impossible disgrace in any
Supply-Labour
event; but merely because 36 per cent is low does not make 62 or 65 per cent an adequate figure. I want to suggest as strongly as I can to the Minister that he should really seriously consider whether this is not the appropriate time to enunciate these same strong trade adjustment principles that have been accepted and enacted in many other parts of the world. I suppose the Government has made up its mind, and nothing that anyone on this side of the House can say will change it, but I do feel that it is embarking on a very serious trend which will result in a lot of needless quarrelling and tension between organized labour and Government in the future.
The automotive workers union I thought made some very reasonable proposals to the Government when they met, and I want to place them on the record. They have six points which, if accepted, would have assured their complete co-operation, instead of what is now their outright opposition. First of all they wanted preferential hiring of displaced workers to ensure that those who lost their jobs as a result of the program would be given every possible assistance to remain in the industry, and not lose seniority, pension, vacation and other credits, as well as the level of wages they had achieved in the industry. What is unreasonable about that? It seems to be a perfectly proper submission to make.
Second, they wanted an eamings-related adjustment benefit payable during the period of transfer from one job to another, or during the period of retraining. What is unreasonable about that?
We have met that.

Yes, but very niggardly, and in a way in which everybody but the Government is convinced is hopelessly unfair.
Third, they wanted transfer allowances covering the cost of transportation of the displaced worker and his family, as well as his furnishings, to a new location after he is reemployed, or to a training centre away from home. What is unfair about that? What is unfair about asking, if you are going to be moved as a result of Government action, to be compensated for the cost entailed? Why should the worker bear that cost?
Fourth, they asked for federal Government action to end discrimination in hiring practices in the industry, so that older workers who may be displaced will not be refused employment. Again, what is unreasonable about that? I should like to hear from the

June 30, 1965
Supply-Labour
Minister as to why the Government could not accept that proposal.
Fifth, they asked for Federal Government initiative to obtain management co-operation in having advance notice of major changes in the levels of employment in the auto and auto parts industry, in order to minimize the effects of dislocation. Again, what is unreasonable about that? Why should they be told on a week end that 500 men are going to be laid off?
Finally, they asked for supplementary pension benefits payable to older displaced workers who may be retired early. Again, that is a reasonable proposal which, if it had been accepted, would have assured the co-operation of the trade union movement.
As I have said, many of these proposals have been accepted in other parts of the world and in other jurisdictions. Had they been accepted here, this scheme could be launched with the support of the trade union movement instead of in the face of what appears at the moment to be its bitter opposition.
Our second objection, aside from the inadequacy of the allowances, is the veto power that is given to the companies. Today on orders of the day we asked the Minister whether or not the companies would be required to make contributions to the TAB fund and the Minister quite candidly, as is the case, admitted that there was no requirement for other than voluntary payments on behalf of the companies. It is not good enough for the Minister,-and we are not going to pass this item until we get an answer-to get up and tell us that he does not anticipate having such a problem placed before him. We all know that the Minister never anticipated having to bring in this program, because when we first began to ask questions months ago we were told there would be lots of employment, no dislocation and that no one had to worry. It was not until the United States union representatives appeared before a Congressional Committee and urged it to put pressure on Canada to bring in an adjustment assistance scheme, that any action was really obtained, and I have the transcript of the statements that were made at that time.
It is not enough for the Minister to get up and tell us that he does not think there is any problem and that the companies will pay. We want to know what is going to happen, what your plans, proposal and programs are going to be in the event that the motor companies decline to make these payments. As the hon. Member for Ontario has said, they

are pretty tough cookies. It is very hard to get even the SUB plans put into agreements. I do not think they are necessarily going to run down here with $700,000 or $800,000 and hand it over to the federal treasury. We want to know what will happen in the event this takes place.
Finally, we should like to obtain some information from the Government as to why nothing has been done to ensure that the price cuts or savings to the companies are passed on to the consumer in the form of some kind of lower prices. I know the companies have stated that they intend to use this money for expansion, but all the indications we can see in the press from statements that have been made that there is going to be no price reduction, and no benefit to be passed on to the consumer at least for the foreseeable future. I could quote, although we do not want to hold this item up, many of the articles that have appeared in such papers as the Financial Post, the Globe and Mail, the Windsor Star, Time and other periodicals -which all indicate there is going to be no price cut passed on to the consumer.
This is a completely indefensible position, because of the very substantial profits that are amassed by these Canadian companies. According to one estimate, the annual average profit of the automobile manufacturers has often run to about 30 per cent of their net worth; that is the total amount of their investment capital, compared with the normal 10 to 15 per cent. One Federal official has estimated that in a good year the profit earned by one of the leading Canadian auto producers might run as high as 80 to 90 per cent of its investment capital.
These companies have money coming out their ears, and do not require the $50 million bonanza in order to finance their expansions. They have lots of money, and there is no reason in the world why some action cannot be taken toward lowering the price of cars. We have made a rough estimate and feel that it would be possible to have an immediate price cut of about 4 per cent in the wholesale price, and that this could be followed by other cuts at a later date.
* (4:40 p.m.)
This would eventually result in a 17 per cent reduction in the price of cars to Canadians. If the companies refuse to pass this on, the Government has the simple expedient of lowering the tariff payable by individuals who buy cars in the United States; and this, of course, would immediately force the companies into price reductions.
June 30, 1985

In summary, Mr. Chairman, we again want to emphasize the general desirability of the objectives, and we again want to urge the Minister that he reconsider the level of benefits, because this action will likely set a pattern for almost all of our trade adjustment figures in the years ahead. Unless the level is substantially increased you will engender hostility and lack of co-operation among the trade movement generally in Canada.
We would like to see some form of requirement placed in the legislation so that the companies will be obligated and required to make these contributions. We simply do not feel it is good enough to leave it on a purely voluntary basis and to trust in the social conscience of Ford, General Motors and Chrysler, because to my knowledge they have never displayed any great sense of social responsibility except at the urging of the trade union movement. Finally, we would hope that the Government would take some action to pass on the price savings that the companies are enjoying to the Canadian public.
Shall the resolution carry?

Before the resolution carries, Mr. Chairman, the Minister was asked a direct question by the hon. Member for Ontario with regard to whether there was any possibility in the Minister's mind that this measure would apply at some time in the future to the textile industry and the steel industry. I wish to add to the industries mentioned by the hon. Member the rubber industry, the clothing industry and the shoe industry. I have been sent here by my people to look after their interests, and since there are quite a few companies in my riding of the types I have mentioned I should like to ask the Minister if he contemplates the possibility of extending the privileges of this measure to these other industries?

Mr. Chairman, may I make a few comments in reply to remarks made by hon. Members. First of all, there is no class of workers whose benefits under the TAB plan will be lower than under a SUB plan. The TAB benefits will generally be greater. In the case of workers in automobile parts plants who are not covered by SUB plans the total TAB benefit payment will be paid out of this fund to a maximum amount of close to $75 per week at present. This is not a copy of the American plan. The purpose of my visit to Washington was to find out in fact what the American plan was and to exchange views
Supply-Labour
with the Secretary of Labour of the United States on our respective approaches to these plans.
We expect that the benefits will be paid by the Unemployment Insurance Commission. The TAB benefits will be retroactive to the beginning of any lay-off and there will not be a 30 day waiting period as suggested by the hon. Member for Ontario, but a waiting period of one week which he suggested is provided under SUB plans.
With respect to the points made by the hon. Member for Danforth, it is a fact that we are breaking new ground in establishing this plan in Canada. It is a very important new step. We are taking the lead in this direction. This is the first time it has ever been done. Our plan is as good as the United States plan and compares favourably with any such plan anywhere in the world. We have accepted the proposal of the United Automobile Workers that we develop an earnings related transitional benefit program. In addition, the duration of benefits will extend up to a year, and for workers in training an additional six months of TAB benefits will be provided so that the maximum will be a year and a half. We are also making available to the workers grants for relocation, as was announced in our mobility program. Any workers dislocated under this agreement will be eligible for the grants under our new mobility program.
We have accepted in great measure the proposals put forward by the United Automobile Workers and I venture to suggest that once this plan is fully understood by the automobile workers there will be much less resistance than was suggested by the hon. Member for Danforth, because we are putting forward in Canada a plan at least as good as that put forward in the United States and there is no indication that in that country the automobile workers or unions will oppose the plan. At least, they have not done so to this point. I venture to suggest that when this plan is fully understood and the built-in benefits for the workers are fully understood, support for the plan will increase.

Mr. Chairman, as the Minister knows the American plan is not settled yet and is still before various committees. I do not want to go into the figures because of that fact, but if it should turn out that the American plan provides higher benefits once their scheme is completed and the final figures are drawn, would the Minister be prepared to amend the Canadian legislation then, so they would conform?

June 30, 1965
Supply-Labour

No, Mr. Chairman. We could not accept the view that our policy should be determined by the final outcome of the policy in the United States. We could not do that in the Department of Labour or elsewhere. At the moment, however, as we see their plan developing our plan is as good, and I think definitely superior in certain aspects with respect to protections for workers, because under our proposal the SUB fund and the SUB credits for workers will be fully protected and not used up, and thus will be available for subsequent lay-offs. This is a very important point that is not covered in the United States. The companies are also requested to come forward to assist in the transition, which is not being done in the United States, although it has been asked by leading members of the Congressional Committee.
The hon. Member for St. Hyacinthe-Bagot has asked about the application of this new lead to other situations in the country. That is a matter of Government policy which is under consideration and any decision in this regard will be announced in the usual way.

Mr. Chairman, I want to ask the Minister a question about the estimate on unemployment. I want to say that this supplementary vote and the other one brought in by the Minister of Industry, which has just been dealt with, ought to be called two items for the repair of the damage done by the Minister of Industry who in his haste concocted an agreement without looking fully into what the effects of the agreement would be. When this agreement, which was signed by the Minister of Industry on behalf of the Government and never referred to Parliament, was first made public we drew attention to the fact that there were three groups of people to whom some attention would have to be paid.
[DOT] (4:50 p.m.)
The first were the workers who would be unemployed and would suffer economic dislocation; second, the small parts manufacturers who would have to retool their plants or relocate them, and third, the consumers of Canada who are losing some $50 million a year because of the access given United States cars and parts into Canada, and who have a right to expect cheaper cars.
Now, the first two calamities have come about, the unemployment and dislocation of the small parts manufacturers. Unfortunately, we have not seen the third effect, which is

an improvement in the price of Canadian cars. I think it will be quite a while until we see any improvement in that direction. I regret that both the previous item, with which we dealt, and this one have been brought into the House merely as supplementary estimates. It seems to me we ought to have had legislation so that there would be spelled out on the statute books the precise terms and conditions under which these various plans will operate. Both of them are going to operate on an ad hoc basis, with very little detailed information except what we can collect in this short period when these two items are before the Committee of Supply.
I want to protest most vigorously this method of dealing with such an important question as the dislocation of hundreds of workers in the automobile industry, without any legislation and without any real information as to the kind of plans which the Government has devised in the hope of providing some amelioration during this dislocation period. I wanted to ask the Minister something about the $5 million estimate. Has the Department of Labour or the Department of Industry made any estimate of the total number of workers in the automobile industry who are likely to be unemployed as a result of this agreement? Has the Minister any information as to the average length of time this unemployment is likely to continue? Has the Minister's department made any estimate as to the total amount of money that will be required? Is this $5 million simply a figure pulled out of the air, just as the Minister of Industry did in providing an estimate of assistance to the small parts manufacturers, or is it based on any figure as to how many persons are likely to be unemployed? I should like the Minister to give us some idea of the research that has been done in this field. We want to know whether or not this $5 million is adequate and over what period of time it is likely to be needed.

I will be frank with the hon. Member and say it is difficult to make any precise estimate because of the pattern of the lay-offs, which is difficult to determine. As an illustration, I may say that the projection of lay-offs by the Ford Motor Company changed at times from week to week. We have attempted to make estimates of the cost, for example, of the Ford lay-off, but they are just as good as the assumptions about the length or duration of the lay-off and the number involved, and these change very quickly.
June 30, 1965

We have thought that for this year we are likely to be taking care of the situation more than adequately by providing $5 million. It certainly will meet any situation that may arise in this year. A yardstick for a precise forecast as to the pattern of lay-offs is something that cannot be provided, because the automobile companies have not fully determined their plans and the parts companies have not yet fully felt the effects of the automotive agreement.
We are now meeting, through this, the temporary dislocation but we are keeping in mind, of course, as the hon. Member will appreciate the additional benefits to the inindustry and to the economy through this increased production and employment. It is for this reason we thought it reasonable that public funds ought to be spent to assist the workers. I cannot give a more precise estimate than that, for the reasons I have given.

I agree fully with the Minister that public funds ought to be spent to help workers, if this rationalization of the automotive industry is going to benefit the economy as a whole, as we hope it will. Certainly, in that case, the economy as a whole has to make a financial contribution to any of those who are going to suffer economic loss as a result of this rationalization process.
I should like to know to what extent the automobile industry is going to contribute to this. All I have been able to gather from the Minister's remarks is that the automobile industry will only contribute if it chooses to do so, by making payments into the Government fund on the same basis as it would have paid into SUB, which it would be required to do under the collective bargaining agreement. What I have not had clearly explained yet by the Minister is what the Government does in the event the Ford Motor Company decides not to participate. As I understand it, any company which does not have a collective bargaining agreement containing a provision for SUB, then a payment under TAB will be made to those employees. Where a company has a SUB provision in its collective bargaining agreement but does not make payments into the Government fund, what is the position of the workers then? I know the Minister said a short time ago he did not want to be flippant and say this was a hypothetical case, but we have to deal with hypothetical cases. The Government is asking us to approve a sum of money to be spent under certain terms and conditions. We want
Supply-Labour
to know what is going to happen to these workers. It is not really a hypothetical case.
If one may judge by this morning's press, the Ford Motor Company is making somewhat hostile noises about this plan. We are not sure whether or not they are going to co-operate with the Government. I have not been able to understand from what the Minister has said why this plan should not be compulsory. The automobile companies are getting $50 million a year in benefits. The taxpayers of Canada were not asked about this and Parliament was not asked about it. It has been compulsory so far as we are concerned. The workers who are laid off find that it is compulsory for them. Nobody asked them if they wanted to be laid off or wanted this plan approved. I see no reason why the companies should not be required to co-operate by making their SUB payments to the Government fund. I want to ask the Minister, if a company decides to exercise its option and not co-operate, what position will the Government take? What is the position of the workers, because it is the workers about whom I am concerned in this matter? [DOT] (5:00 p.m.)

Mr. Chairman, when I rose a few minutes ago I was not paying close enough attention to what you had been saying; I was listening to my advisers. But I will correct that for the future.
On the subject of interim supply I propose dealing with the situation which has come to a head in Canada recently, based on the findings of the Dorion inquiry.
I think this is one of the most serious problems that has faced our country; it is

June 30. 1965
Interim Supply
perhaps the most serious in the history of our country. There may have been other instances in the past when Parliament was disturbed and the country upset over problems within Government circles, but I believe this is the first instance in our history when there appears to have been a creeping encroachment of international crime into high circles in government; and this is cause tor alarm among all Canadians. As far as I am concerned, it is the major point of the whole trouble. It was mentioned by the Prime Minister himself last night, rather belatedly, recognizing the fact that, as he put it, we must deal with the sinister and growing involvement of crime in politics.
[DOT] (5:20 p.m.)
Before dealing with some of the factors I should like to express my appreciation of the action taken throughout this very difficult and trying period by a man whom I have not met, but whose name has been mentioned here, at the inquiry and in the papers, Mr. Pierre Lamontagne, the lawyer in Montreal. I think he has shown, under extraordinarily difficult circumstances, a devotion to duty and to the cause of justice that is highly creditable. The pressure that he was subjected to, as appears from a reading of the report of Mr. Justice Dorion, is an indication that only a man of sterling qualities could have resisted that pressure. He is a credit to his profession and a credit to Canada.
I quote from page 99 of the report, just to indicate the pressure he was under in the opinion of Mr. Justice Dorion:
It none the less becomes perfectly clear that this intervention by Mr. Letendre-
Who occupied a very prominent position as Executive Assistant-
-greatly contributed to heighten the impression on Mr. Lamontagne's mind that influential persons responsible for the government of this country were concerting their efforts to lead him to agree to the release of Lucien Rivard on bail.
You could not gain any other impression if you read the record of the constant telephone calls, interviews and suggestions-suggestions that people high up in the Government were concerned with Mr. Lucien Rivard. And Mr. Lamontagne resisted those pressures.
I want to pay my compliment to the hon. Member for Yukon who brought this matter to the attention of the House of Commons and to the public of Canada. I was present in the House on November 23, 24 and 25 last year when the hon. Member raised the issue, and I recall very well how he asked the

This is the extent of the message that I am trying to get across to committee members, and I say that it is an indictment of the actions of the minister that he has not referred this matter to the proper law officers of the crown, to whom it should have been referred, to obtain their opinion. It is an indictment of the minister to have acted with the commissioner of the R.C.M.P. in a judicial capacity, which is not his function. The Honourable the Minister of Justice, before reaching a decision, should have submitted the case to the legal advisers within his Department with instructions to complete the search for facts if necessary and secured their views upon the possible perpetration of a criminal offence by one or several of the persons involved.
The vindication of the hon. Member for Yukon is complete. He did on that occasion what I hope any hon. Member would do under similar circumstances-he disclosed a situation that required cleaning up. He took his chance in this House, as many people have to do when they deal with topics which are unpopular at the time, but he had the courage of his convictions, laid the case before the House of Commons, endured the cries from the other side of "Smear", "Innuendo" and "McCarthyism", and endured for the last seven months a type of persecution which has been carried on with people connected with Government circles. This is the type of service for one's country that deserves commendation, because, Mr. Chairman, in the background of all this is a narcotics case. There is nobody in this country who has not a horror of the dope peddling which goes on. We are aware of the ruination of young lives that results from this terrible traffic. This is the shadow which was cast over the whole investigation and over the whole problem-the shadow of drug peddling, of narcotics, that carries with it the destruction of human lives. That destruction starts, as we have read so many times in newspapers and in magazine articles, with our younger people.

I want to intervene to move the matters under discussion to something that may appear to many Members of the House far less interesting and dramatic, and I am inclined

to think it is less interesting and dramatic a subject. However, I believe it is a subject that has to be mentioned in this debate because it is a matter of considerable constitutional importance and a matter which the Government ought to have brought before this House by way of resolution. I refer to the proposed amendment of the British North America Act to add a new Section 71 A, reducing the powers of the Legislative Council of Quebec.
Members of this Committee will not need to be reminded that under the terms of the British North America Act, Section 92, the right to amend the constitution of a province is clearly given to the provincial legislature. If the Quebec legislature had acted, therefore, the matter would not be one which concerned this Parliament in any way at all. However, the Quebec legislature has not acted. Section 71 of the British North America Act clearly sets out that the Legislature of Quebec consists of two houses, one styled the Legislative Assembly and the other styled the Legislative Council. The Legislative Assembly recently passed an Act called the Quebec Parliament Act, which provided in effect that any money bill passed by the Legislative Assembly may go into effect one month after its passing, even if the Legislative Council has not accepted it. Bills, other than money bills, can go into effect after a longer period of delay if passed by the Legislative Assembly, without any regard whatever to the Legislative Council. In this matter, the council was willing to accept the restriction of its power, the clipping of its wings, except in two cases, one relating to the rights of minorities and the other where the constitution of either Canada or of the provinces was being dealt with.
Now, Mr. Chairman, these suggested compromises were not accepted by the Legislative Assembly of Quebec. The Lieutenant Governor of Quebec, therefore, at the instance no doubt of the cabinet of that province has transmitted to the Governor General an address seeking an amendment to the British North America Act, and asked that it be forwarded to the Queen for eventual passage by the Parliament of the United Kingdom. This takes the form of an amendment to the British North America Act, and the then Acting Prime Minister, the Secretary of State for External Affairs, told us on June 16 that this was being forwarded with the advice that action be taken on it.
Now, Mr. Chairman, in our view there are very serious and erroneous precedents

being established by this course of action. It is very clearly set forth in the White Paper that was filed by the Government itself just a few weeks ago relating to the amendment of the Constitution of Canada. This is a survey of the whole matter and was made under the direction of Hon. Guy Favreau, Minister of Justice, and dated February, 1965. At page 15 two principles were stated. I quote:
The first general principle that emerges in the foregoing resume is that although an enactment by the United Kingdom is necessary to amend the British North America Act, such action is taken only upon formal request from Canada. No act of the United Kingdom parliament affecting Canada is therefore passed unless it is requested and consented to by Canada. Conversely, every amendment requested by Canada in the past has been enacted.
I ask the House to note the second general principle which is stated here, and I quote:
The second general principle is that the sanction of Parliament is required for a request to the British Parliament for an amendment to the British North America Act. This principle-
This is referring to the sanction of Parliament.
-was established early in the history of Canada's constitutional amendments, and has not been violated since 1895. The procedure invariably is to seek amendments by a joint address of the Canadian House of Commons and Senate to the Crown.
There you have it, Mr. Chairman. In a statement put out by the Minister of Justice just a matter of three or four months ago reviewing this whole matter, it is stated with the utmost clarity that the principle that you only do this with the consent of Parliament has not been violated since 1895. Now, without any reference to this House whatever, it is proposed that we violate a principle that has been established and set out in this clear way.

I know that the Secretary of State for External Affairs took the view before, as he suggested in his question, that this statement of principle is not applicable. He says that the matter only affects the Province of Quebec. But, Mr. Chairman, on the face of it that is not a correct statement. When an amendment is sought to the British North America Act it requires the intervention and advice of the federal executive, and the Parliament of Canada is involved. A very dangerous precedent is set when amendments to the Constitution of Canada are made on the request of the executive alone.
Now, Mr. Chairman, as most Members of the House will be aware, we in this party have no brief at all for second, non-elected chambers. We indeed, have made our views clear a number of times, even in this session when we were discussing the other place and what we thought of its position in the constitutional set-up. However, I want to suggest to this House that constitutions are of fundamental importance and should not be changed by methods of dubious legality and dubious constitutionality. Constitutions are not the possession of an elected assembly alone, subject to immediate change at the request of an executive. In our view the constitution primarily belongs to the people, and we believe the people of Quebec have the right to be consulted.
